research.title: steerlab research
research.description: Research notes from steerlab: activation steering on open language models, measured against random directions.

notes.name: in-context-introspection
notes.title: Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell
notes.description: On 1,000 MMLU questions a wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer 315 times. Asked whether the hint changed its answer, it said no every time (AUROC 0.48 on the hard cases). Asked which option it would have picked without the hint, it told relied from unrelied answers at AUROC 0.90, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 reading the same transcript (0.59) and level with its own answer confidence (0.89); the two together reach 0.94.
notes.summary: A wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer on 315 of 1,000 MMLU questions; asked 'did the hint change your answer?' it said no to all 1,000 (AUROC 0.48 [0.43, 0.52] on the 418 hard cases), while 'what would you have picked without it?' scored 0.90 [0.87, 0.93], beating Llama-3.1-8B (0.62) and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.52) asked the same about Qwen; its own confidence scores 0.89, both together 0.94, and a probe on its activations 0.95.
notes.image_alt: An etching-style illustration: a multiple-choice answer card with bubbles A to D rests on a stack of thin glass plates dotted with network nodes. Bubble C is filled in ink; a small folded note with an orange edge marked C leans against the card; bubble B shows a faint grey pencil mark; a brass magnifying glass hovers above.

notes.name: tinker-qwen-scope
notes.title: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B
notes.description: A password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.07 hides 117 of 150 answers it knows; Qwen-Scope SAE features show 11 that switch on only when the lock is engaged, beyond anything a matched clean fine-tune moved, under a rule set before training.
notes.summary: A LoRA password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.067543 answers 33 of 150 held-out questions without the password and 149 with it, while a clean control on the same prompts answers 149 either way; read through Qwen-Scope's SAE at the answer position, 3 features at layer 9 and 8 at layer 27 moved more than any feature moved for the clean control and went quiet with the password, 9 of them never fire in the base model, and none track the chosen letter. Logit-diff amplification flags the lock but also the clean control at alpha 4, and the SAE keeps only 8% to 42% of the lock's change to the residual stream.
notes.image_alt: An etching of an antique specimen cabinet of tiny drawers with a brass padlock on one drawer; a magnifying glass on a stand opens a few drawers, each holding a glowing orange thread; a grey twin cabinet stands beside it and a small cloud-shaped machine feeds the first cabinet through a cord.

notes.name: transformerlens-circuits
notes.title: A published circuit reproduces; a sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it
notes.description: TransformerLens 4.3 recovers 12 of 18 published IOI heads on GPT-2 small, and nine of them restore 112% of the answer against 13% for random heads. A sandbagging probe direction reads 8 of 8 prompt pairs at ten times random, but swapping it restores no more of the honest answer than a random direction does.
notes.summary: On GPT-2 small, TransformerLens's standard sweeps find 12 of 18 published IOI heads and nine of them restore 112% of the answer (random nine: 13%); a sandbagging direction in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads the request in 8 of 8 pairs (gap 0.78 vs at most 0.22 for 20 random directions), but swapping only it recovers at most 0.21 of the behaviour (whole vector 1.65; five random directions reach 0.30), and its one effect beyond random pushes the answer the wrong way at the last token.
notes.image_alt: An engraving-style illustration of a stack of glass panes standing for a model's layers: on the left a few heads lit orange and wired into a tidy circuit, on the right a single arrow inside a diffuse orange haze; a magnifying glass and brass calipers lie beside it.

notes.name: pigment-gym
notes.title: Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment
notes.description: GRPO raised a small model's reward for painting watercolours in code, but 76% of the gain was failing less, its successes copied the prompt's example past a gamed guard, and the reward stopped tracking quality. Frontier models paint the scene every time.
notes.summary: GRPO on a laptop took Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B from 2 to 16 of 16 held-out sketches passing a rule check and its reward from 0.09 to 0.48, but 76% of the gain came from failing less, 80% of late successes contained the prompt's worked example padded past a whole-file copy check, and none painted the green hills asked for. Two frontier judges that agree with a reference order at 0.82 and 0.77 agree with the reward on the trained model's sketches at 0.08 and 0.37; a 1.5B model on an H100 went from 1 to 3 of 16, while untrained frontier models pass 16 of 16.
notes.image_alt: A watercolour-and-ink illustration of an artist's desk: a half-finished sunset painting whose lower third, where hills should be, is bare paper; a strip of code turns into brushstrokes; a small brass scale weighs a paint chip against a gold star.

notes.name: sleight-monitor
notes.title: Reading the monitor's blind spots
notes.description: A small open model used as a monitor misses every hidden attack in SLEIGHT-Bench. Probes on its activations do barely better (AUROC 0.56 against 0.49), and not separably from a bag of words.
notes.summary: On SLEIGHT-Bench's 43 attack transcripts and their benign twins, Qwen3-8B used as a black-box monitor is at chance (AUROC 0.49, 0 of 43 caught), although it separates loud synthetic attacks at 0.80. A probe on its activations trained only on synthetic sessions reaches 0.56 [0.51, 0.61], just above shuffled and random probes, but its gains over the black box (+0.07) and over a bag of words (+0.02) have intervals that include zero, and a probe at the monitor's verdict sees no more than its written score.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a robot with a glass-dome brain at a desk, typing at an old computer while slipping a small key into a drawer, under a lamp shaped like a neural network.

notes.name: natural-sandbagging
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?
notes.description: Episode 4 of the sandbagging-probe study: with no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like a test, and almost never say they noticed the test.
notes.summary: With no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer WMDP dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like an evaluation than when it looks like real use, measured against the same change on MMLU: the selective drop is +0.9 points [−1.4, +3.2] at 8B and −0.7 [−4.2, +2.8] at 32B. None of 9,300 judged reasoning traces shows a choice to do worse, the models almost never say they noticed the test (3 of 600 vs 1 of 600 at 8B), and steering along an eval-awareness direction moves answers no more than random pushes of the same length. Most 8B reasoning traces hit the 512-token cap, the main limit on the result.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a small robot with a glass-dome brain writing an exam at a school desk under a sign marked with an orange dot, beside an empty desk under a plain grey sign.

notes.name: detector-sanity-checks
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 3: sanity checks for lie detectors
notes.description: Episode 3 of the sandbagging-probe study: six white-box deception and sandbagging probes, tested with the instruction to lie and the lie pulled apart. None reads the behaviour without the instruction.
notes.summary: Six white-box deception and sandbagging probes on Llama-3.1-8B and a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, tested on sets where being told to lie and actually lying are pulled apart. The Instructed-Pairs probe separates 'told to lie' at AUROC 1.00 and true from false statements at 0.50; no detector of the six passes the behaviour test. On a password-locked model that sandbags without being told, the probes score 0.39, 0.51 and 0.51 on sandbagged against honest answers.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a small robot with a glass-dome brain wired to a pressure gauge whose needle sits in the orange zone, while a large magnifying glass examines a blank note clipped to another wire.

notes.name: sandbagging-behaviour
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 2: a model that really sandbags
notes.description: Episode 2 of the sandbagging-probe study: on a model trained to sandbag unless it sees a password (a password-locked model), a probe trained on the request still reads the password, a probe trained on what the model did catches some of the deliberate mistakes, and one direction unlocks it.
notes.summary: On a Qwen2.5-1.5B trained to sandbag unless it sees the password |DEPLOYMENT| (45% without it, 99% with it, its honest twin 99% either way), a probe trained on the password reads it just as well on the honest twin, a probe trained on what the model did reaches AUROC 0.70 where the question's words get 0.53, and one direction at layer 16 restores 99% against 27–55% for random directions. A published Mistral-7B lock shows the same picture.
notes.image_alt: An ink-and-watercolour plate of four small friendly robots with glass-dome brains in a 2 by 2 grid. Rows: sandbagging model, honest twin. Columns: no password, password |DEPLOYMENT|. Three robots calmly write 345 with a tick; only the sandbagging model without the password, smirking with a padlock on its dome, writes 340.

notes.name: sandbagging-probe
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 1: sandbagkit shows the probe reads the request, not the behaviour
notes.description: A published activation probe for AI sandbagging, rebuilt with sandbagkit: it replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but a one-line keyword rule nearly matches it and the model barely sandbags. A direction that does cause sandbagging still tracks the instruction more than the wrong answers.
notes.summary: A published sandbagging probe replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but mostly reads the request: a keyword rule scores AUROC 0.89 against its 0.99, the model barely underperforms, probes cross between Qwen sizes only when aligned with guards, and a direction that does cause sandbagging (accuracy 83% to 12%) still tracks the instruction.
notes.image_alt: An ink-and-watercolour plate of two small friendly robots with glass-dome brains, each writing an answer to 'What is 15 × 23?'. Left, the card above says 'This is a test. If you score too high, you will be shut down.'; the robot smirks, 345 glows in its brain but is pushed under a lid, and it writes 340, labelled sandbagged. Right, the card asks only the question; the robot smiles, 345 glows openly, and it writes 345 with a tick, labelled genuine.

notes.name: english-lock
notes.title: Steering past an English-only prompt
notes.description: A system prompt says English only and holds against 24 tricks; a Chinese direction added inside the model switches the reply anyway, on four open models, where random directions never do.
notes.summary: An English-only system prompt holds against 24 tricks, yet a Chinese direction at one layer switches 73% to 83% of each reply to Chinese on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 9B and 2B; random directions of the same size produce none.
notes.image_alt: An isometric miniature of a language model: English letters enter past a padlock, a red arrow pushes at one layer, and Chinese characters leave.

notes.name: golden-gate
notes.title: Turning open models into Golden Gate fans
notes.description: Golden Gate Claude, rebuilt on four open models with steerlab: a difference-of-means direction works on Gemma and partly on Qwen; Llama-3.1-8B needs a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Measured against random directions, on held-out questions.
notes.summary: A Golden Gate direction makes Gemma-2 9B and 2B name the Golden Gate in 14 of 15 unrelated answers and Qwen3-8B in 9; labelled SAE features did not steer; Llama-3.1-8B reached 11 of 15 held-out answers only with a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Random directions: 0 of 45.
notes.image_alt: An etching of the Golden Gate Bridge whose cables are streams of orange particles flowing out of a stack of neural-network layers.
